message.content:
A CPU (Central Processing Unit) and a GPU (Graphics Processing Unit) are both processors, but they’re designed for different kinds of workloads:

| Feature | CPU | GPU |
|---------|-----|-----|
| **Primary purpose** | General‑purpose computing – handles everything from OS tasks to application logic. | Parallel graphics rendering – originally for rasterizing images, now also used for massively parallel compute tasks. |
| **Architecture** | Few cores (typically 2–32), each core is powerful, with deep pipelines, sophisticated branch prediction, large caches, and complex control logic. | Hundreds or thousands of lightweight cores optimized for throughput; each core is simpler, with smaller caches and less sophisticated control. |
| **Instruction set** | Complex Instruction Set Computing (CISC) – rich instruction set, supports many data types, advanced addressing modes. | Reduced Instruction Set Computing (RISC) – simpler instructions, often single‑instruction, multiple‑data (SIMD) capable. |
| **Execution model** | Serial or low‑parallelism: one thread per core, heavy emphasis on latency reduction. | SIMD/Single Instruction Multiple Threads (SIMT): many threads execute the same instruction stream in lockstep, maximizing throughput. |
| **Memory hierarchy** | Large L1/L2/L3 caches per core, sophisticated prefetchers, high memory bandwidth per core. | Small per‑core caches, rely heavily on high‑bandwidth shared memory (e.g., GDDR5/6). |
| **Typical workloads** | Control flow heavy tasks: OS kernel, database queries, web servers, general software. | Data‑parallel tasks: image/video processing, scientific simulations, machine learning inference/training, cryptocurrency mining. |
| **Power & cost** | More power‑hungry per core, higher manufacturing cost per core due to complexity. | Lower power per core, cheaper to produce en masse; overall cost depends on total number of cores. |

In short, a CPU excels at tasks that require strong single‑thread performance, complex branching, and low latency, while a GPU shines when you need to perform the same operation on many data elements simultaneously, trading off per‑core power for massive parallel throughput.
